The news from India is of so much importance. and so nearly absorbs all the public interest, as to render it necessary to vary tlie usual order of this portion of our paper, and to commence with a hi id statement ot our victories in that quarter of the globe, before we proceed to our usual summary ot home affairs, and ol the pailiamentary business of the week. Our notice of the intelligence from India mav be most conveniently distributed under the three heads ; þÿ ilte cause and local seat ot the war; the leading particulars ol the victory obtained bv 8hr C. Napier; end the policy and probable consequences ol Uiese very critical proceedings. The scat of the war is in the tipper or northern regions of India ; in u e Sc nn e country, approaching very ii'oir to tlie source of the liver Indus. These regions, contain jmr O about one million of inhabitants, anil comprehending both sides of the In ins lor about five or six hundred miles from its sources, are chiefly inhabited by Hindoos, but having been conquered by the Mohammedans some centuries ago, the government ot tlie country has been ever since retained by these fierce Mussulmen loaders. Accordingly, these chiefs, under the name of Ameets, have possessed the provinces amongst them ; most of them being descendants of the eat ly conquerors, and acknowledging one chief, who exercises the supreme ami paramount power at Hyderabad, the capital of Seinde. Now, as these princes and people possessed the whole country on both hanks ol tlie Indus,

from nearly its source to some hundred miles beyond Hyderabad, and as ibis country, down to tlie very banks of the river, is covered with thick forests and jungles, it afforded occasional facilities to these turbulent princes themselves, and at all times to the predatory bands, to attack onr commercial and government vessels in their vovage up and down the river , and thus most vcxatinusly and mischievously to nnnov our commerce and the public service. In order to cut off this source of mischief it was deemed necessary by Lord þÿLlh nborougli and bis council to require the Ameers to make of land lying immediately along the river, in order that the future

navigation of the river m'ght be rendered secure lor the þÿCompany s merchantmen and steamers Major Outturn, ot whom such honourable mention is made in the dispatches, was sent to Hyderabad to make this demand; the Ameers, being resolved not to make this cession, contrived, sav tlie dispatches, to temporise until they could collect tl.eir troops; and having effected this purpose, on the 14th of February last they issued tiieir commands to Major Outrarn to retire from their city, and upon his delay, they attacked his residency on the following day. '1 he residency was gallantly defended by Major þÿOutram s guard of one hundred men, for several hours, when lie effected his retreat to the steamers, and proceeded to join Sir C. Napier, who, with a force of two thousand seven hundred men, was in full march upon Hyderabad. Such was the origin of the war. In tlie other columns of our paper vve have given the despatches so full as to render it needless here to recapitulate them ; we shall therefore coniine ourselves to those few points and heads, which appear chictly to characterise the business. Major Outrarn joined Sir C. Napier, as above said, on February 15. On the following (hi v, the lGih, Sir G Napier inarched to Mutharee, a few miles nearer t« Hyderabad, and there ascci tair.ed that the Ameers were in position at Meeanee, distant about ten miles in tlie latter direction, and to the number of twenty two thousand men. On the followji day, the ISth, Sir G. Napier marched for . vard and took possession of Hyderabad, to which ( d v also the Ameer princes itnmeiiijiteiy followed, and delivered themselves up as prisoners of war. Two points are here chiefly worthy of note : the fim, that this victory was effected by a British and native force of two thousand eight bund i cd men against an enemy of twenty two thousand. CHINA. Our advices from China are to the 21st of January, hut the news is unimportant. Tranquility continued to be preserved in Canton, and the perturbed and discontented spirit which ied to the riot of the 7th December, and which still in some de wee prevailed amongst the popt lace, seer iv to be entirely subdued bv the ptu. m-t to. isttres of the municipal authorities. An attempt to blowup one of the public gams of the city afforded, some time ago, sure evidence of its existence ; but the prompt issuing by the government ol proclamations, couched in a resolute and decided tone, and which had the client of preventing any serious disturbances, proved at the same lime the anxiety of the Chinese officers to rivet the good feeling now so happily subsisting between the two gov. ernments As a f urther proof of the sincerity of our celestial friends, it may he mentioned that m a recent number of the Fehi.n Gazette an announcement is made that the 11 strongest impel iul þÿcommands have been given to the

governors, &c., of the Cite Keatig. Fukecn, and Keaugnan provinces, to use their utmost endeavours for the maintenance of friendly relations. Elepoo, the high imperial commissioner deputed by the Chinese government to conduct the commercial negociations with Sir Henry Pottinger, arrived at Canton on the 10th ol January, and took up his residence ia the city. He immediately apprised the Blent, potentiary of his arrival, and some little correspondence took place between them, wtiea it was arranged that the lirst negociatory conferences should be held at Whampoa about the 21st of January. With respect to the new tariff, nothing has transpired as to the terms which are i;kelv to he recommended for adoption by the merchants, a committee of whom was appointed, ns will he remembered, to advise with Sir Henry Pottinger on the se'iect. The imperial list of duties will, however, it is thought, be the basis of the tariff An application lias been tr ade to Sir Henry, with the view of ascertaining w lien the new arrangement is likely to be carried into execution ; and he lias stated in reply, that þÿ there is no proha bilily ol a change taking place during the present comtnct cial r . >n, :o, all. cue reference to Pekin would be þÿrequisite. When Elepoo reached Canton, the Cong merchants expressed þÿ. .Mr de ire to have an in i tew w ith him, which he d i 1 it ts now said t! ; t he has demand; '.I (tom the; , by next June, the whole amount of their debtx which is to the extent of 3,000.000 dollars.

The claims for indemnification preferred by parties whose property was destroyed during the disturbances of the 7th and 8th ol December, have not yet been settled ; but the ability and firmness of Sir Henry Pottinger, in w hose hands the matter has been left, ate considered a sullic.icni guarantee ft r their satisfactory adjustment. The Chinese officers made direct oilers ol compensation to the aggrieved parties, who, however, deemed the above courses one better calculated to promote tlx :r interests. The river at Canton continues to be infested with pirates to a dneerous extent, and these desperadoes seem daily to grow more daring and audacious in their deeds. Au English lorcha, or lighter, called the Enter prise, lias been attacked and captured ; her cargo, worth 25,000 dollars, plundered, end her captain and officers and four ." - ; ; . », sailors cruelly put to death. Mr. Wilson, a European passenger, tea taster n the (inn of Messrs. Turner and Co , had a hair-breadth escape, as also a Chinese woman, who was on board, and who managed to leap with Mr. Wilson into one of the þÿlorcha boats s when the vessel was set on fire. Home of the wretches engaged in this barbarous transaction are in custody, two of their number having voluntarily confessed the atrocity, under the hope, it seems, of gaining a reward for the assassination of Englishmen, in accordance with the promise publicly made during the war.

From Dell's Weekly Messenger, London April 3, 1813. UNITED STATES, \c. By the Great Western, which arrived at Liverpool on Saturday morning, we have received New York papers to the J6th ult. In communicating to the House of Ktpresentativos the correspondence which has taken place between the British and American governments on the interpretation of that part of the treaty of Washington which relates to the right of search, President Tyler expresses his regret that there is a misunderstanding between the two governments on the subject; he denies that there is any foundation for the right of visitation as claimed by Lord Aberdeen, but intimates that the difference is one of definition rather than of principle. The session has closed without any alteration being made in tiie tariff. The bill for the occupation of the Oregon territory, which had, it will be remembered, passed the Senate, had been left untouched by the House of Representatives. Trade and manufactures are described as stagnant þÿ Money was abundant, there not being any employment for it in business. The legislature of Maryland, one of the insolvent states, had passed a law authorising the sale of the State's interest in certain canals and railways, the proceeds to go in liquidation of the debt of the state. Should the operation succeed, it would extinguish four-filths of the whole debt.

Romance in Real Life. þÿ A case presenting features of more ilian ordinary interest, and strongly illustrating the maxim that crime seldom fails to result in its own punishment, occupied the Insolvent Debtors' Court on Monday, before Mr. Commissioner Barrell. Wo allude to the case of an insolvent named Edward O'Shaughnessy. The facts detailed in evidence ate briefly these: þÿ In 1837 or ISJS O'Shaughnessy, who was understood to be in comfortable circumstances, feigned a passion for the daughter of Halliuan, a girl of prepossessing attractions, and in manners superior to many of her grade, lie won Iter affections but to betray them, and cast his victim a broken-hearted wanderer on the world. Bnder the solemn promise ol marriage, lie overcame her virtue, as it was stated, forcibly þÿ a. id site not being desirous of prosecuting her destroyer, or ot exposing herself to the taunts of her acq mintances, resolved to emigrate to Atactica. She proceeded to the United Stales, wht re she obtained such employment as her industrious habits in farming lilted her lor, but destiny cast O'Shnughnessy again i:i her way. He offered bet marriage, the o.'ior was accepted, and the ceremony solemnized in due form, according to the ritual oi the Catholic Church, by a priest ut Mow York, lie lived but three months with her, when he abandoned her in the midst of strangers, relumed to Ireland, and after some time attempted to many another woman þÿ an attempt which he failed to accomplish through the ministry of

a Catholic clergyman, but in which he was successful by obtaining that ol a protestant clergyman, who was not acquainted with the matter. His first wife, alter having endeavoured without success to support herself in America, was compelled by the pressure of distress to come home and seek an asylum in her father's humble abode. IS he was received with paternal kindness, but llullinan conceived that her husband was bound to support her, and O'Sh.iughm ssy residing in tiio neighbonihood, lie had hint served with a civil- hill process for the maintenance of his wafe. O'tShnuglincssy appeared, and defended the process, lie denied that he had over mariied her, and had well nigh succeeded with Ids defence, when, strange to sa v, two witnesses were forthcoming, who were present in America when the marriage was solemnized between the parties ! They canto forward, deposed to the facts, and went through a scutching ckss examination.

The force of truth, however, prevailed, and p. decree was granted against the double betrayer ! þÿ ' And most strange of all in this eventful history," the debt for which lie was detained in this instance was on a decree for 10/. obtained against him for the support of a child, the fruit of another amour ! The learned commissioner intimated that this tvas one of the most extraordinary cases that had come before him in his experience. WOMAN'S LOVE OF FLOWERS. In all countries women love flowers þÿ in all countries they form nosegays of them, but it is only in the bosom of plenty that they conceive the idea of embellishing their dwellings with them. The cultivation of flowers among the peasantry indicates a revolution in all their feelings. It is a delicate pleasure which makes its way through coarse organs, it is a creature whose eyes are opened, it is a scene of the beautiful, a facullv of the soul which is awakened. Man then understands that there is in the gift of nature a something more than is necessary for existence þÿ colours, odours, are perceived for the first time, and these charming objects have at last spectators. Those who have travelled in the country can testify that a rose tree under a window, a honey suckle around the door of a cottage, are always a good omen to the tired traveller. The hand which cultivates flowers is not closed against the supplications of the poor or the wants of the stranger.

A FAMILY OF FOUR PERSONS MURDERED! A rcpo'. t of the most shocking case of wholesale, butchery that stains the annals of our peaceful state comes to us this morning Irom Warren county. A family of lour persons, consisting oi John Casts eu, wife and ch'.ld. and John 11, Park, (a brother in law,) b ving at Change- Water near Port Colden, on the Morris canal, was found baibarously murdered early yesterday morning, by a neighbor who was passing toward the port lie first discovered the mangled body of Castner in a sink hole on one side of the road, some 2 or 300 yards from the house, to which he hastened with all possible speed, but found no answer to his knock. The other neiuhbors were instantly called, and on throwing open the door the body of Mrs. Castner was futirid, with her murdered infant in Iter arms, lying in bed, killed apparently by stabs in the neck. On going up stairs the neighbors found a hired boy, some 15 or 16 yeais old, in his bed, severely wounded by similar stabs, unable to give any account whatever of the dreadful occurrence, not knowing even how he was hurt, though having possession of his senses. They next entered Mr. Park's room, and also found his body in bed, he having been killed in the same way, apparently by the same instrument. Mr. P. was an unmarried man of some CO years. On returning to the lower story of the house two boys, trom U to 10 years old, Mr. Castner's eldest children, were found asleep in the room adjoining their mother's, perfectly unconscious of the

dreadful tragedy enacted during the night. The whole neighborhood was of course alarmed, and measures were promptly adopt ed to trace the unknown murderers, including a reward of $1000. Money appears to have been the object, as the family was reputed to be r:ch. Mr. Patk, it is said, had dtawn several thousand dollars from the Belvjdere Dank, which were found undisturbed in his closet. Castner's desk was found open, and may have been robbed of more or Ess money, but nothing certain is known about it. Whereas by the laws of the state of New Jersey, the Governor is authorized when any murder is committed within said state by some person or persons unknown, and the same shall be made known to him by the oath of one or more credible persons, to offer a reward not exceeding Three Hundred Dollars for apprehending and securing the person or persons who may have committed such crime: And Whereas it is made known to me by the oaths of such witnesses, that on the night of the first of May instant, four persons, to wit, John B, Parke, John Gastner, Maria Castner, and a child, were murdered at Changewater, in the County of Warren, in litis state, and that the perpetrators of the crime are unknown. The stock, however, of ail kinds <d cotton in Canton on the 1st February is very large, amounting to 109,114 bales, being about double the quantity in Canton at the same time last season. In British manufactures very little has lately been done, chiefly owing to the uncertainty that existed as to the tunc when the new duties and customs regulations would come into operation. But as it is now understood that no change will take place before July, business will be again resumed, and it is expected with more animation in consequence of the removal of this Uncertainty. The stock of grey sheetings is much reduced, large shipments intended for the Canton market having been sent to Chusan and Amoy. White shirtings were also fn demand. Of cotton yarn the stock is very heavy, the lower numbers entirely neglected Owing to the reduction expected in the duty on woollens under the new tariff none are being now sent to Canton, the holders preferring to store them at Hong Kong till the change lakes place. Superior Spanish stripes are quoted at 1. 15 per yard: long ells assorted 7 Spanish dollars; and scarlet, 10 dols per piece. Very little tea has teen bought for some time past, owing in some measure to the expected reduction in the duty, and partly also to the obstinacy with which the teamen hold out for higher prices than can he given with safety under piesent

circumstances. Calcutta þÿ The indigo crop of the season is very favourably reported upon, and the good accounts received of the appearance of the plant have induced some parties to estimate the probable quantity at 110,000 maunds, while others think it will fall short of that considerably. M adras. þÿ Favourable accounts of the cotton farms in Coimbatore have been received. It is estimated from present appearances, that some of the lands will yield as much as 700ib, to 8001b. per acre. Considering the very few articles ot value there are among the exports ol Bombay, the importance of such an addition as silk must be obvious to every one.

A distressing Case of Poisoning. One of the most distressing cases of this sort occurred in this city yesterday. '1 he wile of Mr Jonathan S. Leverich, respecta- a ble mechanic, having been unwell some days, exliili toil evident symptoms of mental alienation on Tuesday. Yesterday morning, after her husband had left for his work, she placed a portion of nisenic in cup a of cullee, telling a daughter about 12 years of age that it was magnesia for the two younger chiluren, and going with them into another room divided the fatal dose between the two little ones and herself. A neighbor coming in soon after, the daughter mentioned that the mother had administered medicine to the two children, and the dreadful fact was soon inferred, when medical aid was immediately procured. It came, however, too late, as the quantity taken rendered all interposition fruitless The eldest child, a boy of 2J years died in less than two hours, the infant aged 8 months, in three, and the mother in nine hours, at about 6 o'clock last evening. Riot at Dantzic. þÿ We learn from the Dantzic Gazette that a serious disturbance took place on the 1 1th and 12th of \ r I , in that city, in consequence of some ol the merchants having transhipped directly to vessels hound for foreign ports a quantity of corn received in boats from the interior of the country. The custom hitherto was, to have the Corn landed and measured, and afterward transhipped to the vessels, by which doutbo operation the workmen gained a larger sum. When they beheld the corn transhipped directly, they assembled on the 1 1th iti crowds on the quays, and all business was suspended. The police interfered, and arrested seme of the ringleaders The next day the assemblages became still greater, and a considerable number of persons proceeded to the police office to demand the liberation of the persons in confinement. This being refused, the rioters spread themselves through the streets, causing terror wherever they appeared. A squadron of hussars then attempted to clear the streets, but the rioters armed themselves with sticks, and evinced a determination to resist. 'Fhe authorities now ordered the drums to beat to arms. One man was shot, others wounded, and several were trampled under foot by the cavalry. When the account left, order had been partially restored.

Remarkable dreams appear to be growing much in favor, of late, in connexion with murders and other events of magnitude. The Philadelphia Inquirer tells this story of one, foreshowing the savage destruction of the Castner family. YVe should think somewhat better of it it it had been made public before the ciime was committed: The following was related to us yesterday by a highly respectable merchant, his inform ant being a resident of the neighborhood in which tire murders were committed. On tbc night of tbe massacre, a highly respectable individual, residing within fifteen or twenty miles of the scene, had a dream, in which all t!u particulars of Stic tragedy were vividly pictured to his mind. It made such an impression upon him that he gave a

detailed statement to several persons the next morning, and for some time before the facts of the real occurrence became known to him and his immediate neighbors. Alter tbe intelligence of the massacre was receive I, ho still repealed the story of bis dream, and on being asked if he could identify the murderers, as ho saw them in his þÿmind eye, s he said " þÿyes, and pointing to a young man of highly respectable connexions, who was visible not far off, while the party were conversing, said Yonder goes one of þÿthem. The statement was communicated to a member of the committee appointed by the citizens ot YVarren county, to investigate everything connected with the murders, who subsequently waited upon the young man named by the dreamer, and addressed him somewhat to the following cflect : þÿ Our section of country has been disgraced by the most frightful of mimes. Tiro þÿAlmighty 1 feel satisfied, will never permit the wretches who were guiltv of such inhuman enormities to þÿescape The young man assumed to all this, and appeared somewhat moved. Thu other continued þÿ We, the committee, arc I

i i þÿ determined to leave no stone unturned in the course of our investigations. Suspicion has been fixed even upon some of those in whom we have heretofore had every confidence. No hall way measures will do, and we have therefore determined that every man within 15 miles shall be summoned to give on account of his whereabout on the dreadful night in þÿquestion. Upon this, so the story goes, the perspiration stood in heavy drops upon the forehead and temples of the young man, and the individual who addressed him felt disposed to attach some importance even to a dream. A-t the time he left, the informant of our friend said a rumor prevailed that the young man alluded to bad been arrested ; the excitement in the neighborhood rendering it necessary that lie should at least be examined.
